Abstract
#

Birkhoff and Pierce asked in 1956 whether C\mathbb{C}C admits a lattice order compatible with the ring operations. The question was answered in the affirmative in 2026, and the structural problem is now to locate the lattice cones among all directed partial orders. Using a transcendence basis of C\mathbb{C}C over Q\mathbb{Q}Q we embed C\mathbb{C}C into a field of Puiseux series F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}} and stratify the directed partial orders by how much of the expansion a rule has to read: five nested conditions A⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒EA \Rightarrow B \Rightarrow C \Rightarrow D \Rightarrow EA⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒E, and six types. A cone satisfying CCC is never a lattice order, so no lattice cone is of Type 1, 2 or 3; and no lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C has 111 as a strong unit, since a lattice-ordered field in which 111 is a strong unit embeds in R\mathbb{R}R, and R\mathbb{R}R has no square root of −1-1−1: the classical Archimedean argument therefore excludes nothing, and every lattice cone is of Type 4, 5 or 6. Type 4 contains lattice cones: the cones of He and of Bao and Zhang are of this type, and so is a cone constructed here from their recursion with a different seed, in which 111 is not positive. Type 6 is not void in the wider class of lattice-ordered fields—Q(2)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})Q(2​) with the cone {a+b2:a,b≥0}\{a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \ge 0\}{a+b2​:a,b≥0} is one—but no cone of Type 5 or of Type 6 on C\mathbb{C}C is known. The group of order units separates the two families: it equals Q>0\mathbb{Q}_{>0}Q>0​ on the cones of Bao and Zhang and is uncountable on the basic order DDD.

Keywords: directed partial order, Puiseux series, valuation, lattice-ordered field, Birkhoff–Pierce problem

MSC 2020: 06F25 (primary); 12J15, 12J20 (secondary)

1. Introduction
#

In 1956, Birkhoff and Pierce asked whether the complex field C\mathbb{C}C admits a lattice order compatible with the ring operations [1]. In 2011, Schwartz and Yang proved that C\mathbb{C}C admits directed partial orders [2], that is, cones PPP with P−P=CP - P = \mathbb{C}P−P=C in the terminology of Definition 2.1, and they later showed that a field admits one if and only if it has characteristic 0 and is either real or of transcendence degree at least 1 over Q\mathbb{Q}Q [3]. For a non-Archimedean totally ordered field FFF, the directed partial orders on F(i)F(i)F(i) compatible with the order of FFF were studied by Rump and Yang [4], by Ma, Wu and Zhang [5, 6, 7], and by Xu and Zhang [8]; Wang, Yuan, Zhang and Zhu [9] added a construction by integral closures of local rings and conjectured that no lattice order exists on C\mathbb{C}C. None of these orders is a lattice order.

That conjecture was refuted by [10, 11], which answered the Birkhoff–Pierce question in the affirmative. In [10], He constructs, for every real t>1t > 1t>1 transcendental over Q\mathbb{Q}Q, a compatible lattice order on C\mathbb{C}C with 0≺10 \prec 10≺1, 0∨i=t0 \vee i = t0∨i=t and 1∧t=01 \wedge t = 01∧t=0, and obtains at least 2ℵ02^{\aleph_0}2ℵ0​ distinct lattice orders, each extending the usual order on Q\mathbb{Q}Q. In [11], Bao and Zhang construct a lattice positive cone PPP from a valuation of value group Q\mathbb{Q}Q and a transfinite recursion of countable ordinal length, with 1∈P1 \in P1∈P, Q>0⊆P\mathbb{Q}_{>0} \subseteq PQ>0​⊆P, P∩Q=Q≥0P \cap \mathbb{Q} = \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}P∩Q=Q≥0​, {x∈P×:x−1∈P}=Q>0\{x \in P^{\times} : x^{-1} \in P\} = \mathbb{Q}_{>0}{x∈P×:x−1∈P}=Q>0​, 0∨i=(t+i)/20 \vee i = (t + i)/20∨i=(t+i)/2 and 0∨(−i)=(t−i)/20 \vee (-i) = (t - i)/20∨(−i)=(t−i)/2, and they show that there are exactly 2c2^{\mathfrak{c}}2c lattice positive cones on C\mathbb{C}C, where c=∣C∣\mathfrak{c} = |\mathbb{C}|c=∣C∣. The existence problem is therefore closed, and the questions that remain are structural: which cones are lattice cones, how the new examples relate to the cones of [2]–[9], and which property of a cone forbids the suprema that a lattice order has to possess.

This paper answers the last question inside a hierarchy. Section 3 constructs directed partial orders from a Puiseux expansion of the complex numbers, without assuming an ordered subfield in advance. Section 4 stratifies all directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C by how much of that expansion a rule has to read, and obtains five nested conditions A⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒EA \Rightarrow B \Rightarrow C \Rightarrow D \Rightarrow EA⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒E together with six types. The central result there is Theorem 4.13: a cone that is insensitive to all the small changes of some pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a) is never a lattice order, so Types 1, 2 and 3 contain no lattice cone. Section 5 supplies the other half. Type 6 is the Archimedean case, and a lattice-ordered field in which 111 is a strong unit embeds in R\mathbb{R}R, which C\mathbb{C}C cannot do: 111 is therefore a strong unit of no lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C, and every lattice cone whatsoever is of Type 4, 5 or 6 (Theorem 5.13). Both cones of [10] and [11] are lattice cones, so by Theorem 4.13 neither of them satisfies condition CCC; §5.2 records the construction of [11] and locates it in Type 4, §5.4 runs the same recursion from a different seed, which gives a lattice cone with 1∉P1 \notin P1∈/P, and §5.3 locates the cone of [10], which is of Type 4 as well.

The contributions can be listed at once. (i) A Puiseux expansion of C\mathbb{C}C that presupposes no ordered subfield, and the cones d(S)d(S)d(S) read off from it (§3). (ii) The stratification itself: five nested conditions and six types, the Covering Lemma, a complete description of the cones of bounded depth as cards satisfying a product and a sum condition, and the theorem that a cone satisfying condition CCC is never a lattice order (§4). (iii) The location of the lattice cones: Types 1–3 are forbidden, 111 is a strong unit of none of them, so the classical Archimedean argument excludes nothing, and the three lattice cones whose type can be computed, namely those of He, those of Bao and Zhang, and a cone with 1∉P1 \notin P1∈/P obtained by running the recursion of Bao and Zhang from a second seed, are all of Type 4 (§5). (iv) Two invariants, the unit interval and the group of order units, which separate the known lattice cones from every cone constructed here without reference to an expansion (§5.8).

The stratification thus explains, after the fact, why seventy years of constructions produced no lattice order: each of them reads one term of a series, or a window of fixed width, or the small changes of a single pair, and all of them fall into Types 1–3. It also matches the shape of the affirmative answers, which prescribe the supremum of the incomparable pair 0,i0, i0,i explicitly: a cone that reads a bounded part of an expansion cannot do that, and by Theorem 4.13 no cone of Types 1–3 prescribes it.

Two limitations must be stated at the outset. First, the structural theorems of Section 4 are relative to the level valuation: condition AAA allows an arbitrary nontrivial valuation of C\mathbb{C}C, whereas Theorems 4.5–4.8 describe the cones of bounded depth only for the valuation given by the fixed expansion. Second, we do not decide when two choices of the transcendence basis, of the transcendental element and of the embedding give the same cone; no equivalence criterion is known to us, and we record the question as an open problem in Section 5.

Theorem 2.1 (Newton–Puiseux [13, Ch. IV, Theorem 3.1]). If kkk is an algebraically closed field of characteristic 000, then k{{s}}k\{\{s\}\}k{{s}} is algebraically closed.

Remark 2.1. Newton computed the expansion of an algebraic function in fractional powers of the variable by the method of the polygon, and the theorem is named after the proof of Puiseux [12]; a modern account of the theorem and of its place in ramification theory is [20, Ch. 2]. 3. Complex Numbers with Puiseux Series
#

In this section we write every complex number as a series and construct the basic directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C. There are three steps: we isolate one transcendental number ttt, we embed C\mathbb{C}C into a field of Puiseux series in s=1ts = \frac{1}{t}s=t1​, and we define positivity by a condition on the first coefficient.

Definition 3.1. The field of Puiseux series over kkk in sss is

k{{s}}=⋃n≥1k((s1/n)). k\{\{s\}\} = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} k\big((s^{1/n})\big). k{{s}}=n≥1⋃​k((s1/n)).

Thus a nonzero Puiseux series is a formal sum ∑qcqsq\sum_q c_q s^q∑q​cq​sq with cq∈kc_q \in kcq​∈k, whose exponents qqq are rational numbers with a common denominator and are bounded below. Fractional exponents cannot be avoided: a square root of sss is not a Laurent series in sss.

Lemma 3.1. There is an embedding of fields ι:C→F{{s}}\iota: \mathbb{C} \to F\{\{s\}\}ι:C→F{{s}} which is the identity on FFF and sends ttt to s−1s^{-1}s−1.

Proof. The set of elements of C\mathbb{C}C that are algebraic over a subfield is an algebraically closed subfield, and it contains every number algebraic over Q\mathbb{Q}Q. If ttt were algebraic over FFF, it would be algebraic over Q(T∖{t})\mathbb{Q}(T \setminus \{t\})Q(T∖{t}), contradicting the algebraic independence of TTT. Thus FFF, which contains Q‾\overline{\mathbb{Q}}Q​, is an algebraically closed subfield of C\mathbb{C}C, and ttt is transcendental over FFF. Therefore there is an isomorphism of F(t)F(t)F(t) onto the subfield F(s)F(s)F(s) of F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}} which is the identity on FFF and sends ttt to s−1s^{-1}s−1. By Theorem 2.1, the field F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}} is algebraically closed. Since every complex number is algebraic over Q(T)\mathbb{Q}(T)Q(T) and Q(T)⊆F(t)\mathbb{Q}(T) \subseteq F(t)Q(T)⊆F(t), every complex number is algebraic over F(t)=F(s)F(t) = F(s)F(t)=F(s); hence C\mathbb{C}C is algebraic over F(t)F(t)F(t). Thus the isomorphism extends to an embedding of C\mathbb{C}C. □\square□

3.1 The Expansion
#

The field C\mathbb{C}C and the field of Puiseux series are different objects, yet an order defined by “the first coefficient” requires every complex number to be a series. The embedding of Lemma 3.1 is a dictionary that translates each complex number into a series and preserves sums and products; after the translation the cone conditions become statements about adding and multiplying series.

We fix an embedding ι\iotaι as in Lemma 3.1 and identify a complex number zzz with the series ι(z)\iota(z)ι(z). Thus every nonzero z∈Cz \in \mathbb{C}z∈C has an expansion

z=∑qzqsq,zq∈F. z = \sum_q z_q s^q, \qquad z_q \in F. z=q∑​zq​sq,zq​∈F.

This is like a decimal expansion. The image of C\mathbb{C}C is an algebraically closed field containing FFF and sss, so for every n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 it contains all nnn roots of the polynomial xn−sx^n - sxn−s that lie in F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}}, and the series s1ns^{\frac{1}{n}}sn1​ is one of them. Thus sqs^qsq and tqt^qtq are complex numbers for every rational number qqq.

Example 1. Let zzz be a complex number with z2=t2+tz^2 = t^2 + tz2=t2+t. It is algebraic over F(t)F(t)F(t) but not a rational function of ttt. Writing t2+t=t2(1+s)t^2 + t = t^2(1 + s)t2+t=t2(1+s) and expanding the square root by the binomial series gives

z=s−1(1+s)1/2=s−1+12−18s+⋯ . z = s^{-1}(1+s)^{1/2} = s^{-1} + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{8}s + \cdots. z=s−1(1+s)1/2=s−1+21​−81​s+⋯.

Thus zzz has the size of s−1=ts^{-1} = ts−1=t and leading coefficient 111, and an order that reads only the first term calls zzz positive. The other solution −z-z−z has the series −s−1−12+⋯-s^{-1} - \frac{1}{2} + \cdots−s−1−21​+⋯, with leading coefficient −1-1−1. The embedding ι\iotaι decides which of the two solutions begins with +s−1+s^{-1}+s−1.

Another simple example is a square root of ttt, namely s−12s^{-\frac{1}{2}}s−21​, which explains why fractional exponents are needed.

The expansion is the notation in which the orders below read the coefficients of a number. By the axiom of choice it depends on the choice of TTT and of the embedding ι\iotaι. We know of no directed partial order on C\mathbb{C}C that is defined without such a choice.

3.2 Level, Leading Coefficient, and Normalized Series
#

A rule that reads the beginning of a series observes two things: where the series begins and with which coefficient. The first is the level, which measures the size of the number and takes the place of the absolute value; it is of no use by itself, since it does not come from an order on C\mathbb{C}C. The second is the leading coefficient.

Definition 3.2. Let z∈Cz \in \mathbb{C}z∈C be nonzero.

  1. The level lev⁡(z)\operatorname{lev}(z)lev(z) is the smallest exponent qqq with zq≠0z_q \ne 0zq​=0.

  3. The normalized series is u=z/slev⁡(z)=∑r≥0ursru = z/s^{\operatorname{lev}(z)} = \sum_{r \ge 0} u_r s^ru=z/slev(z)=∑r≥0​ur​sr, so u0=lc⁡(z)u_0 = \operatorname{lc}(z)u0​=lc(z).

The following properties follow directly from the definition: lev⁡(c)=0\operatorname{lev}(c) = 0lev(c)=0 and lc⁡(c)=c\operatorname{lc}(c) = clc(c)=c for c∈F×c \in F^{\times}c∈F×; lev⁡(sq)=q\operatorname{lev}(s^q) = qlev(sq)=q and lc⁡(sq)=1\operatorname{lc}(s^q) = 1lc(sq)=1 for q∈Qq \in \mathbb{Q}q∈Q; and lc⁡(−z)=−lc⁡(z)\operatorname{lc}(-z) = -\operatorname{lc}(z)lc(−z)=−lc(z). lev⁡(zw)=lev⁡(z)+lev⁡(w),lev⁡(z+w)≥min⁡{lev⁡(z),lev⁡(w)}. \operatorname{lev}(zw) = \operatorname{lev}(z) + \operatorname{lev}(w), \qquad \operatorname{lev}(z + w) \ge \min\{\operatorname{lev}(z), \operatorname{lev}(w)\}. lev(zw)=lev(z)+lev(w),lev(z+w)≥min{lev(z),lev(w)}.

The Birkhoff–Pierce problem asks for a lattice order, so the first question about a new order is whether it is one. The natural pair to test is 000 and iii, which are incomparable by Lemma 2.2. The idea of the test is that an upper bound of 000 and iii must be a “large” number, of negative level, and that among the large numbers there is no smallest one: from any large number one can subtract a number that is still large, and the result is again an upper bound. The following lemma and theorem make this precise.

Theorem 3.6 is a special case of Theorem 4.13, and its proof is the model for the general one.

The proof shows that the set of upper bounds of 000 and iii, which contains ttt, has no minimal element at all. The next section removes the hypothesis on SSS and extends the statement to all orders of certain types. Section 3 uses only that C\mathbb{C}C is an algebraically closed field of characteristic 000 with a transcendence basis T≠∅T \ne \varnothingT=∅ over Q\mathbb{Q}Q. Therefore Theorems 3.3 and 3.6 hold for every algebraically closed field of characteristic 000 and transcendence degree at least 111 over Q\mathbb{Q}Q. The method cannot work for the field Q‾\overline{\mathbb{Q}}Q​ of algebraic numbers, which has no transcendental element from which positivity could be drawn; indeed, Q‾\overline{\mathbb{Q}}Q​ has no directed partial order at all [3].

4. The Stratification on the Complex Field
#

Section 3 produced some examples from the Puiseux expansion of the complex numbers. In this section we attempt to stratify all directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C, including those not given by any series. What is needed is a property that holds for an arbitrary cone and separates the orders we know. The proof of Theorem 3.6 suggests such a property. The basic orders fail to be lattice orders because a positive number stays positive when it is changed a little, so that an upper bound can always be lowered a little. A lattice order must behave differently when it exists. Hence we stratify the orders by their sensitivity to small changes.

4.1 Windows
#

The basic orders read one term of the series. To find more orders and to stratify them, we let a rule read a longer piece of the expansion; the definition of a window makes “the first few terms” precise. The window depends on the normalized series, so its width is measured from the first term of each number and not from a fixed exponent, which allows the windows to be compatible with multiplication. Since the width δ\deltaδ is fixed, the rule reads the same amount of every number.

Definition 4.1. Fix a rational number δ≥0\delta \ge 0δ≥0, the width.

  1. A truncated series of width δ\deltaδ is a finite sum a=∑0≤r≤δarsra = \sum_{0 \le r \le \delta} a_r s^ra=∑0≤r≤δ​ar​sr with ar∈Fa_r \in Far​∈F and rational exponents.
  2. For 0≤ρ≤δ0 \le \rho \le \delta0≤ρ≤δ and b=∑0≤r≤δbrsr∈Tδb = \sum_{0 \le r \le \delta} b_r s^r \in T_{\delta}b=∑0≤r≤δ​br​sr∈Tδ​, the element sρb=∑0≤r≤δ−ρbrsr+ρ∈Tδs^{\rho}b = \sum_{0 \le r \le \delta - \rho} b_r s^{r+\rho} \in T_{\delta}sρb=∑0≤r≤δ−ρ​br​sr+ρ∈Tδ​ is bbb shifted by ρ\rhoρ, with the terms beyond δ\deltaδ deleted.

We write Tδ×T_{\delta}^{\times}Tδ×​ for the group of units. 4.2 Rules and Small Changes
#

Let PPP be a cone on C\mathbb{C}C. For the basic order D=d(Q≥0)D = d(\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0})D=d(Q≥0​) of Theorem 3.3, a number is positive when its leading coefficient is a positive rational number. Multiplying a positive number zzz by 1+ε1 + \varepsilon1+ε with lev⁡(ε)>0\operatorname{lev}(\varepsilon) > 0lev(ε)>0 does not change the leading coefficient, so z(1+ε)z(1 + \varepsilon)z(1+ε) is positive. The classification rests on the observation that an order is described by the small changes z↦z(1+ε)z \mapsto z(1 + \varepsilon)z↦z(1+ε) which can never destroy positivity. The word “small” means that the smallness is specified by a pair.

For an arbitrary cone, with no expansion given, we need a notion of smallness that uses only the field operations. The set a\mathfrak{a}a of small numbers should have two properties: the sum of two small numbers is small, and a small number times a moderate number is small. If RRR denotes the set of moderate numbers, these are exactly the requirements that a\mathfrak{a}a be an ideal of the ring RRR. We ask also that the quotient field of RRR be C\mathbb{C}C, so that any two complex numbers can be compared through a quotient r1/r2r_1/r_2r1​/r2​ of elements of RRR, which allows one small change to act on two positive numbers at the same time. 4.3 The Five Conditions
#

By Section 3, smallness is measured by a series expansion with a valuation, and positivity depends only on the first term or on a window. In this subsection each condition is obtained from the previous one by giving up one requirement.

Definition 4.3. For a cone PPP, let I(P)\mathcal{I}(P)I(P) be the set of all ε∈C\varepsilon \in \mathbb{C}ε∈C such that z(1+nε)∈Pz(1 + n\varepsilon) \in Pz(1+nε)∈P for some z∈P×z \in P^{\times}z∈P× and all n∈Zn \in \mathbb{Z}n∈Z.

Despite the letters, I(P)\mathcal{I}(P)I(P), the set of relative infinitesimals, is unrelated to the valuation ideals IδwI^{w}_{\delta}Iδw​ of Section 3: the former measures the sensitivity of the cone, the latter the size of the elements.

Definition 4.4 (The five conditions). For a cone P≠{0}P \ne \{0\}P={0} on C\mathbb{C}C:

  1. AAA: P=P[mw]P = P[\mathfrak{m}_w]P=P[mw​] for some nontrivial valuation www of C\mathbb{C}C.
  2. BBB: P=P[Iδw]P = P[I^{w}_{\delta}]P=P[Iδw​] for some nontrivial valuation www of C\mathbb{C}C and some δ∈Γw\delta \in \Gamma_wδ∈Γw​ with δ≥0\delta \ge 0δ≥0.
  3. CCC: P=P[a]P = P[\mathfrak{a}]P=P[a] for some pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a).
  4. DDD: P[a]≠{0}P[\mathfrak{a}] \ne \{0\}P[a]={0} for some pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a).
  5. EEE: I(P)≠{0}\mathcal{I}(P) \ne \{0\}I(P)={0}.

Condition AAA is for series expansions whose positivity depends only on the first term. Condition BBB is for series expansions whose positivity depends only on a window of fixed width. Condition CCC says that small changes cannot destroy positivity, for some notion of small; condition DDD says that they cannot destroy the positivity of at least one number. Condition EEE says that there are relative infinitesimals, and its failure corresponds to the Archimedean case.

Definition 4.5 (The six types). A directed partial order PPP on C\mathbb{C}C is of

  • Type 1 if AAA holds (the rule reads only the first term of some series expansion);
  • Type 2 if BBB holds but AAA does not (the rule reads a window of fixed width);
  • Type 3 if CCC holds but BBB does not (for some pair all positive numbers are insensitive to the small changes, but positivity is not described by a window of one valuation);
  • Type 4 if DDD holds but CCC does not (some positive number is insensitive to the small changes, but no single pair makes all positive numbers insensitive);
  • Type 5 if EEE holds but DDD does not (there are infinitely small elements, but every positive number is sensitive to arbitrarily small changes);
  • Type 6 if EEE does not hold (there are no infinitely small elements).

By Theorem 4.12 below, the failure of condition EEE can be read in ordered-group terms as well: EEE fails exactly when no nonzero yyy satisfies ny≤zny \le zny≤z for all n∈Zn \in \mathbb{Z}n∈Z and some fixed positive zzz.

A stratification is only useful if every order is placed in exactly one class. We obtain this because the five conditions are nested: every cone satisfies an initial segment of them and may satisfy none. Their proof is the content of the rest of this subsection.

Definitions 4.2, 4.4 and 4.5, and Theorems 4.4 and 4.12, are stated for cones on C\mathbb{C}C; their definitions and proofs use only the field and cone axioms, and they apply verbatim, with any field containing Q\mathbb{Q}Q in place of C\mathbb{C}C, to cones on that field. They are used in this wider sense below: on Q\mathbb{Q}Q and Q(2)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})Q(2​), on the countable field KKK of §5.3, and on its ultrapower EEE.

Lemma 4.3. For every cone P≠{0}P \ne \{0\}P={0} on C\mathbb{C}C,

A⟹B⟹C⟹D⟹E. A \Longrightarrow B \Longrightarrow C \Longrightarrow D \Longrightarrow E. A⟹B⟹C⟹D⟹E.

Proof. A⇒BA \Rightarrow BA⇒B: take δ=0\delta = 0δ=0, since I0w=mwI^{w}_{0} = \mathfrak{m}_wI0w​=mw​.

B⇒CB \Rightarrow CB⇒C: (Ow,Iδw)(\mathcal{O}_w, I^{w}_{\delta})(Ow​,Iδw​) is a pair by Lemma 2.4.

C⇒DC \Rightarrow DC⇒D: P[a]=P≠{0}P[\mathfrak{a}] = P \ne \{0\}P[a]=P={0}.

D⇒ED \Rightarrow ED⇒E: let z∈P[a]z \in P[\mathfrak{a}]z∈P[a] and ε∈a\varepsilon \in \mathfrak{a}ε∈a be nonzero. For every n∈Zn \in \mathbb{Z}n∈Z we have nε∈an\varepsilon \in \mathfrak{a}nε∈a, so z(1+nε)∈Pz(1 + n\varepsilon) \in Pz(1+nε)∈P. Hence ε∈I(P)\varepsilon \in \mathcal{I}(P)ε∈I(P). □\square□

Theorem 4.4 (Covering Lemma). Every cone P≠{0}P \ne \{0\}P={0} on C\mathbb{C}C with P−P=CP - P = \mathbb{C}P−P=C — that is, every directed partial order — is of exactly one of the Types 1 to 6.

Proof. Let PPP be a directed partial order. Then P≠{0}P \ne \{0\}P={0}. By Lemma 4.3, if one of the conditions holds, then all later ones hold. Thus the set of conditions that hold for PPP is one of {A,…,E}\{A, \dots, E\}{A,…,E}, {B,…,E}\{B, \dots, E\}{B,…,E}, {C,D,E}\{C, D, E\}{C,D,E}, {D,E}\{D, E\}{D,E}, {E}\{E\}{E}, ∅\emptyset∅. These six cases exclude each other and are the types 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 of Definition 4.5 in this order. □\square□

4.4 The Six Types
#

By the Covering Lemma an order is classified by the first condition it satisfies. The rest of this section goes through the types one by one. Types 1 and 2 are described in detail, Types 3 and 4 are exhibited by explicit constructions, and Types 5 and 6 are described by what is known, since they have not yet been explored. Table 1 at the end of the subsection collects the outcome.

Type 1
#

A basic order d(S)d(S)d(S) uses the same set SSS of admissible leading coefficients at every level, but nothing forces this: a general rule reading only the first term may use a different set LqL_qLq​ at each level qqq. We ask which such rules are orders, using the facts that a sum of two numbers of the same level adds the leading coefficients, while a product adds the levels and multiplies the leading coefficients. For the level valuation lev⁡\operatorname{lev}lev of the Puiseux expansion of Section 3 we then describe all cones of depth 0; these form a subclass of Type 1. Condition AAA in general allows an arbitrary nontrivial valuation, and the description below does not cover all such valuations.

A cone PPP has depth 0 (relative to lev⁡\operatorname{lev}lev) if P=P[m]P = P[\mathfrak{m}]P=P[m], that is, if positivity depends only on the level and the leading coefficient.

Type 2
#

The next rule reads a fixed number of further terms, determined by a window. In Type 1, for each level, a set of windows is admissible, and this table is what we call a card. The question is which cards define orders; the answer is again given by two conditions, the direct translations of the requirement that products and sums of positive numbers be positive.

A cone PPP has depth at most δ\deltaδ if P=P[Iδ]P = P[I_{\delta}]P=P[Iδ​]. By Lemma 4.1, this means that positivity depends only on the level and the window of width δ\deltaδ.

Definition 4.6. A card of width δ\deltaδ is a family J=(Jq)q∈QJ = (J_q)_{q \in \mathbb{Q}}J=(Jq​)q∈Q​ of subsets of T×T^{\times}T×, some possibly empty; JqJ_qJq​ is the set of admissible windows at level qqq, and the levels of the card are the qqq with Jq≠∅J_q \ne \emptysetJq​=∅. The rule of the card is PJ={0}∪{z∈C×:win⁡(z)∈Jlev⁡(z)}P_J = \{0\} \cup \{z \in \mathbb{C}^{\times} : \operatorname{win}(z) \in J_{\operatorname{lev}(z)}\}PJ​={0}∪{z∈C×:win(z)∈Jlev(z)​}.

Every cone of depth at most δ\deltaδ is the rule of exactly one card, namely Jq={win⁡(z):z∈P×,lev⁡(z)=q}J_q = \{\operatorname{win}(z) : z \in P^{\times}, \operatorname{lev}(z) = q\}Jq​={win(z):z∈P×,lev(z)=q}. Thus, describing these cones amounts to deciding which cards are valid, that is, for which cards PJP_JPJ​ is a cone.

If a rule reads several terms, one may want it to use the later terms in order to accept, at the same level, both a number beginning with 111 and one beginning with −1-1−1. If that could happen, the first terms of two positive numbers could cancel and their sum could fall at a completely different level, where the card would be useless. The following theorem shows that it never happens. This is the reason why window orders can be described at all, and why each of them lies inside a first-term order.

Type 3
#

Type 3 consists of the orders for which there is a pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a) such that all positive numbers are insensitive to a\mathfrak{a}a, but this smallness cannot be measured by a window of a single valuation. Type 4
#

In Types 1–3 every positive number is insensitive to the small changes of some pair. Type 4 consists of the orders in which this fails for at least one positive number: small changes do not always go unnoticed. To build one we glue together two opposite pieces. For large numbers, of negative level, we keep the first-term rule, which is insensitive; at level 0 we put a rigid set on which no change is allowed, the natural numbers N\mathbb{N}N being the obvious choice, since they are closed under addition and multiplication and have gaps between their elements. The two pieces fit together.

Which types can carry a lattice order? Type 6 consists of the directed partial orders with no nonzero relative infinitesimal, and Type 5 of those that have relative infinitesimals while, for every pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a), every positive number loses its positivity under some change z↦z(1+a)z \mapsto z(1+a)z↦z(1+a) with a∈aa \in \mathfrak{a}a∈a. No order of Type 5 or 6 is constructed here, and none is excluded in general; Section 5 carries the question as far as it goes: no lattice cone is of Type 1, 2 or 3, and the three lattice cones whose type can be computed are all of Type 4. Whether a lattice cone can be of Type 6 is not known, and whether Type 5 is nonempty at all is Question Q2.

4.5 Lattice Orders
#

We return to the Birkhoff–Pierce problem. In Theorem 3.6 the supremum of 000 and iii failed to exist because an upper bound could be lowered by a number that is small compared with it in the expansion. The Wiggle Lemma 2.3 isolates what a supremum would need: a single nonzero change ddd that can be added to and subtracted from both differences h−xh - xh−x and h−yh - yh−y at once. Condition CCC always provides such a ddd, by Lemma 4.2(3), and it does so for every pair, without any expansion.

Theorem 4.13. Let P≠{0}P \ne \{0\}P={0} be a cone on C\mathbb{C}C satisfying condition CCC. Then two complex numbers have a supremum for PPP only if they are comparable, and PPP is not a lattice order.

Proof. Let P=P[a]P = P[\mathfrak{a}]P=P[a] for a pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a). Suppose that x,yx, yx,y are incomparable and that h=x∨yh = x \vee yh=x∨y exists. By Lemma 2.3, p=h−xp = h - xp=h−x and q=h−yq = h - yq=h−y are positive and [−p,p]∩[−q,q]={0}[-p, p] \cap [-q, q] = \{0\}[−p,p]∩[−q,q]={0}. Since P[a]=PP[\mathfrak{a}] = PP[a]=P, Lemma 4.2(3) applies to the positive elements ppp and qqq and produces a nonzero d∈[−p,p]∩[−q,q]d \in [-p, p] \cap [-q, q]d∈[−p,p]∩[−q,q], a contradiction; hence no two incomparable numbers have a supremum. By Lemma 2.2, for p∈P×p \in P^{\times}p∈P× the numbers 000 and ipipip are incomparable, so PPP is not a lattice order. □\square□

When small changes go unnoticed, any upper bound of two incomparable numbers can be lowered slightly and remain an upper bound, so no least upper bound exists. This is the core of Theorem 3.6, where the upper bound hhh of 000 and iii was lowered by ta2t^{\frac{a}{2}}t2a​. Theorem 4.13 needs no hypothesis on the set SSS of first coefficients. The order HHH of Type 4 is not a lattice order either, by Theorem 4.11. So none of the cones constructed in Sections 3 and 4 is a lattice order, and Theorem 4.13 says that no cone of Types 1–3 ever is. The cones of Types 4–6 are thus the only candidates, and Section 5 reduces the list further: a lattice cone is of Type 4, 5 or 6, and both known lattice families, as well as the cone of Proposition 5.8, lie there.

5. Lattice Orders in the Stratification
#

The Birkhoff–Pierce question is settled: C\mathbb{C}C carries lattice positive cones, at least 2ℵ02^{\aleph_0}2ℵ0​ of them by [10] and exactly 2c2^{\mathfrak{c}}2c by [11]. What the stratification of Section 4 can still do is to say where those cones sit, and why no earlier construction reached one. This section proves that no lattice order on C\mathbb{C}C is of Type 1, 2 or 3, and that 1 is a strong unit of none of them; every lattice cone is therefore of Type 4, 5 or 6, and the classical Archimedean argument excludes none. It then computes the type of the cones of [11], constructs a lattice cone in which 1 is not positive, records the bookkeeping of the nonempty types, and introduces two invariants of a cone that separate the new cones from the ones constructed here.

5.1 The Affirmative Cones
#

We recall the two constructions in the language of this paper. Both [10] and [11] are preprints from 2026: we treat them as establishing the existence of the cones, while the details of the constructions await independent confirmation. One step of [10, Theorem 5.1] has been flagged as incomplete in public commentary; the step is repaired in Lemma 5.4 of §5.3, with a full account of what the proof of [10, Theorem 5.1] uses it for, and we use the construction of [10] freely below. Both preprints remain unrevised as of this writing, so all statements about their cones rest on the constructions as announced; no specific step of [11] has been flagged. In [10] a compatible lattice order is produced for each real t>1t > 1t>1 transcendental over Q\mathbb{Q}Q, with 0≺10 \prec 10≺1, 0∨i=t0 \vee i = t0∨i=t and 1∧t=01 \wedge t = 01∧t=0, by valuation rings, extension of bases in infinite dimensional vector spaces, and extension of embeddings; at least 2ℵ02^{\aleph_0}2ℵ0​ orders arise, all extending the order of Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

The construction of [11] is the second affirmative answer, and it carries a theory of its own: a valuation with value group Q\mathbb{Q}Q, a height, and a transfinite recursion that extends a lattice order layer by layer. We state its main theorem in our notation and locate it in the stratification in §5.2.

What the two cones have in common is what matters here: both prescribe the supremum of the incomparable pair 0,i0, i0,i, and Theorem 4.13 shows that no cone of Types 1–3 can do that. The cone of [11] is in addition rigid on units, the positive elements with positive inverse being exactly the positive rationals [11]; whether the cone of [10] has the same property we do not know. We return to the point in §5.8. The two cones also share their type: both are of Type 4, by Propositions 5.2 and 5.7, although the proofs have nothing in common, one using the layers of a height and the other the monad of a lattice order.

The cones of [2]–[9], and those of Sections 3 and 4, are of a different shape: their positivity is decided by the leading term of an expansion, by a window of fixed width, or by the requirement that a single ideal of moderate numbers act as small changes, which is exactly the shape of condition C. Theorem 4.13 therefore gives a uniform reason for the fact, checked case by case in [2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9], that none of those orders is a lattice order; in the cases covered by our types the reason is a proof, and in the remaining cases it locates the obstruction.

#

The point of the stratification is unchanged: these cones are of none of Types 1, 2, 3, so the conjecture of [9] was refuted by a cone of a shape that the stratification does not forbid.

The first affirmative answer, [10], does not read a series, and its construction has two stages of very different character. The first stage builds a lattice order on a countable field by a basis extension; the second transports it to C\mathbb{C}C through an ultrapower and an isomorphism. The two stages behave in opposite ways, and it is the second that decides the type of the resulting cone: the first is of Type 6, the second is not.

Two consequences belong to the ledger. All three lattice cones whose type can be computed are of Type 4: those of [10] and [11] by Propositions 5.7 and 5.2, and the cone of Proposition 5.8. And the argument of Lemma 5.6 is not special to these cones: a lattice cone that contains 12\frac{1}{2}21​ and has a nonzero monad always satisfies D, so a lattice cone of Type 5 or of Type 6 must have a trivial monad or must keep 12\frac{1}{2}21​ out of its cone.

The insensitive element of Type 4 is found one layer higher, at t2t^2t2, and it is found in both cones.

5.5 The Cones of Wang, Yuan, Zhang and Zhu
#

The proposition recovers, and explains, Proposition 2.7 of [9], which states that 0 and iii have no least upper bound in any of these orders. Uniformity is the point of the stratification. Their argument is written for one family and for one pair of elements; Theorem 4.13 gives the same conclusion for every cone that reads a bounded number of terms, and for every pair of incomparable elements.

The comparison also explains why the conjecture of [9] had to fail, and why it could look true. A lattice cone has to be insensitive instead, either to all the changes of some pair or to the changes of some pair applied to one of its positive numbers, which forces it into Types 4, 5 and 6; the cone of [11] sits in Type 4 by Proposition 5.2, and Section 5.4 shifts the same construction to a lattice cone with 1∉P1 \notin P1∈/P, also of Type 4.

5.6 Type 6 and the Archimedean Property
#

Type 6 is the case I(P)={0}I(P) = \{0\}I(P)={0}. By Theorem 4.12(2) this says that no nonzero yyy satisfies ny≤zny \le zny≤z for all n∈Zn \in \mathbb{Z}n∈Z and some fixed positive zzz; for a lattice order it is the Archimedean property, and the classical theorem then applies. Two lemmas prepare it. The first removes the sign of 1 from the discussion, and the second states the classical theorem in the form in which it is true.

Lemma 5.10. Let PPP be a cone on a field KKK. Then −1∉P-1 \notin P−1∈/P. Consequently 1∈P1 \in P1∈P, or 1 is incomparable with 0.

Lemma 5.10 shows that 1∈P1 \in P1∈P is the only alternative to 1 being incomparable with 0: every total order, and every cone that contains 1, satisfies it. A lattice order does not have to contain 1, by Remark 5.1(i), so the strong-unit hypothesis of Lemma 5.11 is substantive in both its parts.

Lemma 5.11. Let KKK be a field with a lattice cone PPP such that 1 is a strong unit of PPP. Then the order is total, and KKK is isomorphic, as an ordered field, to a subfield of R\mathbb{R}R; in particular I(P)={0}I(P) = \{0\}I(P)={0}.

Proof. Step 1: the totally ordered case (optional, subsumed by Step 2). For x∈Kx \in Kx∈K the set {q∈Q:q≤x}\{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q \le x\}{q∈Q:q≤x} is nonempty, because −n≤x-n \le x−n≤x for nnn large, and it is bounded above by hypothesis; so ϑ(x)=sup⁡{q∈Q:q≤x}\vartheta(x) = \sup\{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q \le x\}ϑ(x)=sup{q∈Q:q≤x} and ψ(x)=inf⁡{q∈Q:x≤q}\psi(x) = \inf\{q \in \mathbb{Q} : x \le q\}ψ(x)=inf{q∈Q:x≤q} are real numbers with ϑ(x)≤ψ(x)\vartheta(x) \le \psi(x)ϑ(x)≤ψ(x). Then ϑ\varthetaϑ is strictly increasing: if x<yx < yx<y, choose nnn with 1/n<y−x1/n < y - x1/n<y−x and m=min⁡{k∈Z:x<k/n}m = \min\{k \in \mathbb{Z} : x < k/n\}m=min{k∈Z:x<k/n}, so that x<m/n≤x+1/n<yx < m/n \le x + 1/n < yx<m/n≤x+1/n<y, whence ϑ(x)≤m/n<ϑ(y)\vartheta(x) \le m/n < \vartheta(y)ϑ(x)≤m/n<ϑ(y). Step 2: the general case. Without totality the two cuts need not coincide, and they are replaced by the value theory of lattice-ordered groups; this argument covers the totally ordered case as well, so Step 1 is retained only for its elementary directness. Every convex ℓ\ellℓ-subgroup MMM of KKK is an ideal of the ring: if 0≤a∈M0 \le a \in M0≤a∈M and b≥0b \ge 0b≥0, then b≤nb \le nb≤n for some nnn by hypothesis, so 0≤ab≤na∈M0 \le ab \le na \in M0≤ab≤na∈M, and ab∈Mab \in Mab∈M because MMM is convex. If it were not, some uuu would be neither positive nor negative, and then u+=u∨0u^+ = u \vee 0u+=u∨0 and u−=(−u)∨0u^- = (-u) \vee 0u−=(−u)∨0 would both be positive, with u+∧u−=0u^+ \wedge u^- = 0u+∧u−=0; in an ℓ\ellℓ-group, c∧d=0c \wedge d = 0c∧d=0 implies c∧nd=0c \wedge nd = 0c∧nd=0 for every n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 [16, Ch. XIV], so no multiple of c=u+c = u^+c=u+ dominates d=u−d = u^-d=u−. The strong-unit hypothesis is what the classical theorem needs, and it cannot be dropped. On Q\mathbb{Q}Q with its usual order it holds, and the order is total and of Type 6; the same holds on any field, since the embedding makes the order Archimedean, and then I(P)={0}I(P) = \{0\}I(P)={0} by Theorem 4.12(2). On Q(2)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})Q(2​) with the cone {a+b2:a,b≥0}\{a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \ge 0\}{a+b2​:a,b≥0} the order is a lattice order and, by Lemma 5.5 applied to the basis {1,2}\{1, \sqrt{2}\}{1,2​}, I(P)={0}I(P) = \{0\}I(P)={0}, yet 1 is not a strong unit—2\sqrt{2}2​ is incomparable with every integer—and the field embeds in no subfield of R\mathbb{R}R carrying this order. On C\mathbb{C}C the hypothesis fails for every lattice cone, as the corollary records.

Corollary 5.12. No lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C has 1 as a strong unit. The classical Archimedean argument therefore excludes no lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C.

Proof. If 1 were a strong unit of a lattice cone PPP on C\mathbb{C}C, Lemma 5.11 would embed C\mathbb{C}C in R\mathbb{R}R as an ordered field, but R\mathbb{R}R contains no element whose square is −1-1−1, while i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1. □\square□

5.7 Where the Lattice Orders Are
#

Theorem 5.13. Let PPP be a lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C.

  1. PPP is not of Type 1, 2 or 3; hence every lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C is of Type 4, 5 or 6.
  2. 1 is not a strong unit of PPP; hence the classical Archimedean argument excludes no lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C, and Types 4, 5 and 6 all remain possible.

Proof. (1) A cone of Type 1, 2 or 3 satisfies condition C by Lemma 4.3, and no cone satisfying C is a lattice order by Theorem 4.13; the Covering Lemma 4.4 then leaves Types 4, 5, 6. (2) is Corollary 5.12. □\square□

Part (2) says that the check demanded by the classical theorem is not a check at all: no lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C passes it—in the cone of [11] the element ttt has height 1 and no argument of that paper bounds it by an integer, and the corollary shows that no argument ever will—so the Archimedean route excludes nothing. Type 6 is nevertheless excluded for the two known families, by the direct computation of condition E in Lemma 5.3 and Proposition 5.7, and Question Q1 below asks whether it is nonempty at all. The cone of [9], which is not a lattice cone, satisfies condition E as well, since I(P)=tO≠{0}I(P) = t\mathcal{O} \ne \{0\}I(P)=tO={0} in its own notation [9, Theorem 3.1].

Corollary 5.14. No cone of Types 1, 2, 3 is a lattice order, and no cone on C\mathbb{C}C in which 1 is a strong unit is one either, by Corollary 5.12. Consequently the cones of [10] and [11] are of Type 4, 5 or 6; Propositions 5.7 and 5.2 sharpen this to Type 4 in both cases, and by Lemma 5.6 no lattice cone with 12∈P\frac{1}{2} \in P21​∈P and a nonzero monad is of any other type.

Corollary 5.15 (Nonemptiness). Types 1, 2, 3 and 4 are nonempty, by Theorem 4.5 and the constructions listed after it, Theorem 4.9, Theorem 4.10 and Theorem 4.11 respectively, and Type 4 contains every lattice cone whose type is known, by Propositions 5.7, 5.2 and 5.8. No cone of Type 5 or of Type 6 on C\mathbb{C}C is known; but Type 6 is not void in the wider class of lattice-ordered fields: the cone {a+b2:a,b≥0}\{a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \ge 0\}{a+b2​:a,b≥0} on Q(2)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})Q(2​) is a lattice cone with no nonzero relative infinitesimal, and so is the coordinate cone of §5.3 on the countable field KKK. The class of lattice-ordered fields is therefore not confined to Type 5 either, and the question whether Type 5 is nonempty is the question whether some cone has relative infinitesimals while no positive number of it survives all the changes of a single pair.

The remaining alternative is worth stating in terms of the definitions, since it is the only place where the last two conditions still do work.

Remark 5.2. Types 4 and 5 differ by condition D: a cone is of Type 5 exactly when it has relative infinitesimals and, for every pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a), every positive number zzz has a small change z(1+a)z(1+a)z(1+a) with a∈aa \in \mathfrak{a}a∈a that destroys its positivity. So a lattice cone is of Type 4 exactly when some pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a) leaves one of its positive numbers untouched, and Proposition 5.2 shows that the cone of [11] is of this kind: the pair of the height valuation leaves the whole layer H2H_2H2​ untouched, since a change of negative height alters only the terms below the leading one. What had suggested the opposite is the rigidity of these cones on units; but rigidity on units concerns the elements with positive inverse, while the insensitive elements of Type 4 are found among the large ones. Lemma 5.6 isolates the mechanism: a lattice cone that contains 12\frac{1}{2}21​ and has a nonzero monad satisfies D through the pair formed by the bounded elements and the monad, so a lattice cone avoids Type 4 only if one of these two hypotheses fails. The expectation that the lattice cones are of Type 5 is therefore false; the question that remains is the one asked in Q2, whether Type 5 is nonempty at all.

5.8 Two Invariants of a Cone
#

A stratification is the more useful the more of its information can be read off from the cone alone, without a chosen expansion. Two such invariants are available, and they separate the affirmative cones from those of Types 1–3.

Definition 5.1. Let PPP be a cone on C\mathbb{C}C with 1∈P1 \in P1∈P. The unit interval of PPP is [−1,1]P={x∈C:1+x∈P and 1−x∈P}[-1, 1]_P = \{x \in \mathbb{C} : 1 + x \in P \text{ and } 1 - x \in P\}[−1,1]P​={x∈C:1+x∈P and 1−x∈P}, and the group of order units is U(P)={x∈P×:x−1∈P}U(P) = \{x \in P^\times : x^{-1} \in P\}U(P)={x∈P×:x−1∈P}.

  3. U(D)=D×U(D) = D^\timesU(D)=D× for the basic order D=d(Q≥0)D = d(\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0})D=d(Q≥0​), so U(D)U(D)U(D) is uncountable; [−1,1]H={−1,0,1}[-1, 1]_H = \{-1, 0, 1\}[−1,1]H​={−1,0,1} and U(H)={1}U(H) = \{1\}U(H)={1} for the cone HHH of Theorem 4.11; and U(P)=Q>0U(P) = \mathbb{Q}_{>0}U(P)=Q>0​ for the cones of [11].

Proof. (1) If x,y∈P×x, y \in P^\timesx,y∈P× have x−1,y−1∈Px^{-1}, y^{-1} \in Px−1,y−1∈P, then xy∈Pxy \in Pxy∈P and (xy)−1=x−1y−1∈P(xy)^{-1} = x^{-1}y^{-1} \in P(xy)−1=x−1y−1∈P; and x−1∈U(P)x^{-1} \in U(P)x−1∈U(P) for x∈U(P)x \in U(P)x∈U(P), because (x−1)−1=x∈P(x^{-1})^{-1} = x \in P(x−1)−1=x∈P. Hence U(P)U(P)U(P) is a subgroup of C×\mathbb{C}^\timesC× containing 1. (3) For x∈D×x \in D^\timesx∈D× the coefficient lc⁡(x)\operatorname{lc}(x)lc(x) is a positive rational and lc⁡(x−1)=lc⁡(x)−1\operatorname{lc}(x^{-1}) = \operatorname{lc}(x)^{-1}lc(x−1)=lc(x)−1 is one as well, so x−1∈Dx^{-1} \in Dx−1∈D and U(D)=D×U(D) = D^\timesU(D)=D×, an uncountable set. 5.9 Open Problems
#

Three questions remain.

(Q1) Is Type 6 nonempty on C\mathbb{C}C? Equivalently, is there a directed partial order on C\mathbb{C}C with no nonzero relative infinitesimal? By Theorem 4.12 the condition is precisely that no nonzero element is infinitely small with respect to a positive one, for lattice cones the classical obstruction is absent: by Corollary 5.12 no lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C has 1 as a strong unit, and Proposition 5.8 shows that the failure of boundedness is not exceptional, since 1 bounds no positive number at all. The type is not void: on Q(2)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})Q(2​) the cone {a+b2:a,b≥0}\{a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \ge 0\}{a+b2​:a,b≥0} is a lattice cone of Type 6, as noted after Lemma 5.11, and so is the coordinate cone of §5.3 on the countable field KKK, while the cone {0}∪[1,∞)\{0\} \cup [1, \infty){0}∪[1,∞) on Q\mathbb{Q}Q is of Type 6 without being a lattice. What is open is whether C\mathbb{C}C admits one. Lemma 5.5 supplies a sufficient condition, a Q\mathbb{Q}Q-basis of C\mathbb{C}C whose products have nonnegative rational coordinates, and no such basis is known; the constructions of §5 do not supply one, since the three lattice cones are of Type 4 and the ultrapower of a cone with 1∈P1 \in P1∈P always has a nonzero relative infinitesimal. The basis that [10, Theorem 5.1] builds on KKK is of exactly this kind, so the question is whether a positive basis on a countable subfield extends to one on C\mathbb{C}C; the obstruction is purely the passage to uncountable dimension, since a transfinite construction of length c\mathfrak{c}c would have to keep the structure constants nonnegative at limit stages. Formal realness is not the obstacle either: KKK contains iii and carries the lattice cone PKP_KPK​ with I(PK)={0}I(P_K) = \{0\}I(PK​)={0}.

Nor can an answer be modelled on the classical picture of Archimedean ordered fields, for no cone on C\mathbb{C}C is totally ordered, by Lemma 5.10 with Lemma 2.2: a Type 6 cone on C\mathbb{C}C would be a genuinely partial order without relative infinitesimals. Whether some cone of Type 6 on C\mathbb{C}C exists at all, and whether a lattice cone can be one, are both open.

(Q2) Is Type 5 nonempty? For lattice cones the question splits into two concrete conditions by Lemma 5.6: a lattice cone can escape Type 4 only if its monad is trivial or if 12∉P\frac{1}{2} \notin P21​∈/P, and each condition can be attacked separately. In general, by Remark 5.2, the question is whether some cone has relative infinitesimals while no pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a) preserves the positivity of a single one of its positive numbers. The three lattice cones whose type can be computed are of Type 4, so the expectation that the lattice cones are maximally sensitive is false as stated.

(Q3) When do two choices of (T,t,ι)(T, t, \iota)(T,t,ι) and of the cone SSS on the constants give the same cone? No equivalence criterion is known to us, and without one the description of Types 1 and 2 in Section 4 counts cones with multiplicity, once for every expansion that describes them. A criterion of the shape of the one obtained in [9] for generators of cones from integral closures would turn the stratification into a classification.
